analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a MALWARE probability of 0.685, which is above the decision threshold but not decisive. All 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, but the individual SHAP contributions are small and tightly clustered (+0.0057 to +0.0127), so no single feature dominates. Most of the n-grams are generic x86 control-flow and stack-management sequences: SUB PUSH (+0.0127), CALL PUSH (+0.0112), ADD PUSH (+0.0112), MOV PUSH (+0.0109), PUSH CALL (+0.0105), POP PUSH (+0.0065), POP CALL (+0.0068), MOV LEAVE (+0.0068), and CALL RET (+0.0105). These are typical of function prologues, epilogues and argument passing in any compiled C/C++ program, and the evidence lists no functions, API calls, or strings tying them to mining. The more specialized sequences are rare: CDQ MOV (freq 0.000107), SBB INC (0.000090), LEA MOVSD.REP (0.000251), DEC JZ/DEC JNZ (about 0.0009-0.0010), and XOR PUSH / POP XOR. They could loosely fit arithmetic, bulk memory initialization, or counter-driven loops of the kind seen in hashing code, but they also occur in ordinary code. The evidence contains no distinctive cryptographic or mining signatures such as rotate/shift-heavy mixing or SIMD sequences. The overall picture is a modest statistical lean toward malware, with no concrete, traceable cryptojacking behavior, so the result is inconclusive.

All top-20 SHAP contributions are small and tightly clustered, with no dominant feature
Top n-grams are generic stack and call-convention patterns (SUB PUSH, CALL PUSH, MOV PUSH, PUSH CALL)
Rare arithmetic or loop sequences (CDQ MOV, SBB INC, DEC JZ/JNZ, LEA MOVSD.REP) are only weakly suggestive
No function names, API calls, or hashing-specific instruction patterns are present in the evidence
analysis.recommended_action: Treat as suspicious but unconfirmed. Do not classify as cryptojacking on this evidence alone. Run further analysis on the binary: check for mining-pool strings or stratum protocol indicators, examine network behavior, and look for hashing routines with rotate/shift-heavy or SIMD loops. Sandbox it and monitor sustained CPU usage. Cross-check against threat intelligence and hash reputation before a final verdict.
